utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries were announced. Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zupljanin. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Zupljanin. Mr. Zupljanin, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You'd find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And good morning to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just kindly ask the usher to provide Mr. Zupljanin with his statement. Show it to the Prosecution first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zupljanin, for the record, kindly tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Slobodan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have on our screens, 1D1710, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In front of you on the screen as well as in hard copy before you, Mr. Zupljanin, is a document. Can you see a signature there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I do. I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now go to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see a signature on this page and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I see a signature, and it is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have had occasion to go through the statement. Is it the statement you provided to the members of Mr. Mladic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. This reflects the contents of the statement I gave on the aforementioned date to the members of the investigations team.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does it accurately reflect what you told the members of the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: The contents do reflect what I said to the members of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the statement accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Everything I touched upon in my statement is accurate and truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions here today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: In principle, the contents would be the same. Perhaps the word order or sentence structure would not be identical, but the contents would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would offer this statement of Mr. Zupljanin into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01710 receives Exhibit Number D887, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D887 is admitted. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic, if you have any further questions or if you want to read a summary of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would have one or two questions, and I would first read a summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Slobodan Zupljanin testifies about the military and political situation in the municipality of Kotor Varos. In autumn 1991, he was mobilised in the 122nd Light Infantry Brigade which was deployed in Croatia. On 18th of March, 1992, the brigade was transferred back to Knezevo, B and H. He was the commander of the 5th Company of the brigade deployed in Maslovare village, Kotor Varos municipality. At that time, the brigade was composed of the active Muslim and Croat officers. The task of the brigade was to prevent interethnic conflicts, disarm paramilitaries, and keep road communications open. Slobodan Zupljanin states that some incidents broke out in April 1992. Kotor Varos was surrounded by Muslim and Croat villages. From the military point of view, Kotor Varos was encircled. Slobodan Zupljanin witnessed that Muslim and Croats moved around the town and villages carrying automatic weapons freely. He knows that Muslims and Croat had fought in Croatia and had gained military experience. He negotiated the surrender of weapons. Some of the villages surrendered weapons, such as the Muslim villages of Garici and Siprage, and the Croat village of Zabrdje and those villages remained untouched throughout the war. Mr. Zupljanin personally took part in negotiations with Muslims and Croats to ease tensions and avoid conflicts. During one of these attempts he was wounded in an ambush set by Muslim-Croat formations. There were no combat activities at that time. His driver was also wounded and another negotiator was killed. Mr. Zupljanin was present when the Muslim-Croat brigade from the area of Kotor Varos numbering 300 fighters surrendered to the 22nd Infantry Brigade. The enemy soldiers were then transferred to the Republic of Croatia in 26 buses. Mr. Zupljanin's unit was tasked with securing the reception of the Muslim-Croat units, disarming them, and seeing them off from Kotor Varos. Other units were tasked with escorting them. Everything was done without incident. Mr. Zupljanin also took active part in the area of Vlasic by receiving more than 5.000 civilians and 1500 soldiers of Croat ethnicity who had left Travnik and Bugojno, fleeing from Muslim forces. His unit was in charge of receiving these Croat civilians and soldiers. Mr. Zupljanin's unit secured food, medical care, and accommodation for them. And that was the statement summary of Mr. Zupljanin. I will have just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zupljanin, we could see in your statement that you were wounded and you were treated in hospital and at home. You were wounded on the 25th of June, 1992. How long did your convalescence last?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I was wounded early in the morning on the 25th of June, 1992. I was operated at the military medical centre in Banja Luka. At the time, there were many wounded and injured. For a while, I even had my bed placed in one of the hospital corridors rather than in a room because they were overcrowded. As far as I remember, I spent about a fortnight in the hospital. The overall treatment and absence from the unit lasted around three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Following your wounding and during the treatment, did you, nevertheless, have to go in the field; and why, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: In principle, while I was being treated due to my injuries, I was regularly visited by a physician from the battalion medical corps because my wounded needed to be dressed for a long time. In July, I think, I was still immobile, lying down, because I had received wounds to both my legs, upper leg and lower leg on the right side and the left upper leg were wounded. As I said, I was regularly visited by brigade representatives. Often the commander himself came to visit inquiring into my health situation. The first time I left home, if I remember well, was in mid-August 1992. Two soldiers came, one of them a battalion driver and another soldier, and told me that on that morning, the 14th of August, 1992, there was a massacre committed over Serb soldiers in the sector of Vigoste. Muslim fighters from Vecici village on the stretch of road between Obodnik and Vasiljevica Brdo, in the area of Orahe [phoen] village and Vilaste stream, intercepted our van taking people for regular rotation as well as food that was regularly being brought to the positions. Given the fact that it was one of the few vehicles that travelled between Maslovare and Kotor Varos, it often carried civilians as well. That morning, I was told that there were 27 people in the van of whom 13 were killed and 14 were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I was told that there was much panic among the Serb soldiers and local population. They asked whether, with their assistance, I could go to the bridge at the Vigosta river, some 3 to 4 kilometres away from the incident, so as to give support to the panicking soldiers and those who were wounded, trying to ease the situation in a way. I didn't have to think twice. My family members helped me get dressed, and then with the assistance of the two soldiers and with some aids, I managed to get into the vehicle and reach the location. By that time, the -- some soldiers and locals had gathered there, as well as some people I didn't know. The situation was rather heated. One of the people present there in a military uniform and had an M-48 rifle on him but I couldn't recognise him as a member of my unit, as I could confirm later, threatened me personally. He pointed his rifle at my chest, thinking that I was responsible for what had happened to our soldiers. He said that we were being too mild with the enemy. However, the situation relaxed somewhat. There were no further incidents. The soldier with the rifle withdrew. Some other people came to the location in the meantime and we tried to explain to them that whenever there's an enemy in front of you in a combat area, any kind of scenario is possible. I think that morning we managed to defuse the situation so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, focused questions usually do not take answers of five minutes which go in every direction. Could you please try, if you want to examine the witness, to keep a certain focus on what we should hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin, did you address the civilians as well and what kind of mood was theirs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I addressed them too. There were some cries for revenge and suggestions of going against the Muslim population immediately so as to avenge our losses. However, that day, we managed to prevent any such thing from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zupljanin. That would be all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Ms. Bibles, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin, you'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Bibles. You find Ms. Bibles to your right. Ms. Bibles is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If the Prosecution could please have 65 ter 31901. We can start off with page 1 on both.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 7 of your statement, you describe the transition of your unit from the JNA to what would become a VRS unit; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I discussed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, the article that has come up on the screen in front of you was written in 1994, and it's a retrospective about the 2nd Battalion. Do you recognise this article?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't recall having seen this article before.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, in the first paragraph, this describes a formation of the battalion on 7 May 1992 and it describes: "Serbian young men rushing to report." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I see it, but it wasn't that the people were rushing. They were simply responding to a draft call.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now the second paragraph starts with a line: "The minarets of Vecici mosques trembled at the mention of the Maslovare Chetniks gathering in Borje." Now, your battalion was a Serbian military unit from the very beginning in May of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: In principle, it was a Serb army unit. Although, at the time, there was Captain First Class Nijaz Vrabac who was a member of the unit, he commanded a platoon of mortars, as well as Alojzije Gasparevic, who was the commander of the Mixed Antitank Artillery Unit. It was a smaller unit that had the Zis cannons at its disposal. He had commanded a unit in Slavonia and then returned to the battalion. The assets of his unit were sent to Vlasic. Of course, at some point --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: -- I can't recall when, they did leave the battalion, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you agree that the battalion, your battalion, the 2nd Battalion, was a military unit to support the Serbian -- Serbian republic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't fully agree. I do agree in part though. It was a battalion that had been a part of the JNA and after that, it became part of the Serbian Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then part of the VRS. The tasks of the battalion were crystal clear. We were there to support the overall population in the area of Kotor Varos municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, on the third page in English and I believe it's the second page in the original, we'll be looking at a series of villages that are listed at the bottom of -- in the English version, it's the first paragraph. Sir, we're looking for a list of places in which the 2nd Battalion was involved and includes Hrvacani, Vrbanjci, and Vecici. Do you see that list of villages?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: It concerns the locations you mentioned. In other words, parts of the battalion units were somewhere in the general sector of those villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you agree that your battalion, the 2nd Battalion, engaged in all of the locations listed in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion was engaged in disarming paramilitary formations as well as in protecting the population and preventing the incursions of any sabotage and --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: -- scouting units from the Lasva valley, as well as to protect their road.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, that was not the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Could you look at the list of villages at the bottom of that paragraph and tell me whether you or your battalion or portions of your battalion were engaged in all of those locations between 1992 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You find in the column in the middle of this page, in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I saw the list. The unit or parts of my battalion were not in the area of Sokolina and Visevica. As for the other village, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 65 ter 31901.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31901 receives Exhibit Number P7089, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to discuss the matters that were left out of your witness statement and that is the 1992 events in Vecici and Grabovica. In paragraph 15 of your witness statement, signed on the 4th of July, 2014, you indicate that your battalion was relocated to the area of Vlasic in early November 1992. Would you agree that this is the same time-frame in which the killings in Grabovica occurred in November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: The battalion was relocated to the area of Vlasic following the events in Grabovica in 1992. The first unit --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: The issue of the resistance of Vecici in Kotor Varos was an important military issue to the VRS from July to November 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was an important military issue as well as an important civilian issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you would agree that the people who surrendered at Grabovica in November 1992 were fleeing from Vecici; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I learnt that those people had left Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Would -- we're now going to play a small portion of a video, P850. The portion we'll play involves VRS actions in Kotor Varos in July of 1992. I would like for you to watch and then after the video, I'll have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: For the booths, we'll start the video at page 2 in both language transcripts about halfway into Reporter Ajder's comments. I believe it is starting with: "Yesterday and today the air force ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the transcripts already been revised or should we play it twice?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I believe we can just play it once, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's in evidence, that's true. Therefore, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, we're beginning at 3:59 in the video as it's marked.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... and special police units ... the air force of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina also participated and targeted enemy targets. The number of fatalities among the Muslim-Croat paramilitary has exceeded 300, with a significantly greater number of wounded. In yesterday's and today's combat alone Muslim and Croat extremists had over 100 wounded and killed and about 200 wounded. Their own civilians, Muslim women, children, and the elderly, are held hostage by the extremists who tortured and killed them. Yesterday, between 1600 and 1700 hours, in the vicinity of Rujevica village, on the road between Maslovare and Kotor Varos, enemy villains tortured and bestially killed Stevan Markovic and Obrad Bubic. They also killed Milan Stevilovic and captured Nova Petrusic. A commemoration ceremony was held today in honour of Milan Stevilovic at the Banja Luka Yugoslav People's Army Hall."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for the record, we've stopped at the video at 4 minutes, 52 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, in this video, we saw combat aircraft bombing a village. Do you agree that this village was Vecici?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I believe so. I believe it is the village of Vecici that is depicted on the footage. But I have to say that at that time I was in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Well, sir, you would agree that these were VRS aircraft; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I learned later from my visitors to the hospital those were aircraft of the Serbian republic -- or the Army of Republika Srpska or the JNA. I don't know whose aircraft it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know where these aircraft would have -- or planes would have been based?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in July of 1992, the VRS air force was commanded by General Ninkovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I think that I can confirm that it was indeed General Ninkovic. His name came up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you would agree that in order to have air-strikes like we observed in the video, someone on the ground would have been giving details up the chain of command to reach the aircraft; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand your question. Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'll see if I can make this more clear. The air force of the VRS would have bombed this particular location with the assistance of the field units in Kotor Varos; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I was not in the unit at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So moving on to after you returned to your unit, you and your battalion took part in different operations involving Vecici; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: The battalion, yes. I was not involved in Vecici at all because I was not in the unit on the 29th of June when there was an operation in Vecici. Neither was I there in the month of July when paramilitary formations in Vecici were being disarmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, apparently there may be some misunderstanding but you're referring to a time when the witness had returned to the unit, whereas the witness says: What you described was something that happened before I returned to my unit. Could you please seek to clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, the time-period that I'm describing would be after you returned to service in August 1992 until November of 1992. Were you or any portions of your battalion involved in operations involving Vecici during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: During that period, there was no combat until the moment people left Vecici. At that time, the area was mopped up. In late October, there were negotiations at the requests of the soldiers and civilians of Vecici who wanted to negotiate the conditions of surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have P440 on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You'll see that this is an order for combat operations signed by Colonel Novakovic. And, sir, Colonel Dusan Novakovic was the commander of the 1st Light Kotor Varos Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And in late October, early November 1992, you were the commander for the 2nd Battalion of the 22nd Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Correct. However, the 2nd Battalion was not on the strength of the 1st Light Croatia Brigade. I did not receive my orders from Commander Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm trying to clarify that. So you commanded the 2nd Battalion, Colonel Novakovic commanded the 1st Light Kotor Varos Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And both of these units were within the Operational Group Vlasic headed by Janko Trivic; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So you reported directly to Janko Trivic as did Colonel Novakovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. However, I was subordinated to Colonel Trivic as the battalion commander, a battalion which was part of the 28th Brigade commanded by Novakovic. And Novakovic was in charge of a brigade that was part of the OG whose commander was Trivic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could you please clarify the name, Novakovac or Novakovic, which is the right one?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: It appears to be correct in the transcript Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Is that the name, the proper name of the individual who headed the 1st Light --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Dusan Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have it correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we go to the last page of this order which would be page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S, we see a list of military units. Now, these units that we see to the left and below the signature would have fallen under the command of Colonel Novakovic as parts of the 1st Light Kotor Varos Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And we see the Grabovica command [sic] about halfway down this list. Now they were based there Grabovica; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say "Grabovica command" or "company"?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Company, I'm sorry. Yes. That should be in the transcript, at line 24 on temporary transcript 16, "Grabovica Company." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, sir, was this unit based in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: According to what I know, the Grabovica Company was deployed in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And was the commander of the Grabovica Company at that time a man named Mile - and I'll spell the last name - K-l-j-a-j-i-c?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I'm sure that it wasn't Mile Kljujic. But there was an officer in the 1st Light Infantry Brigade whose name was Mile Kljajic. It may have been him, but I don't know that for a fact because company commanders followed brigade command orders and changed often.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know how many men were in the Grabovica Company?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I really can't tell you. I don't know whether they were on full strength at the time. I suppose that the company had approximately 100 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, 100 men. Is that -- was that your answer, that you supposed that they had 100 men?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I said that I assumed that there were 100 given the formation of the Light Infantry Company. And I suppose that at that time the -- they had what they were supposed to have according to their formation, about 100 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now going back on this document to page 1 in the English and B/C/S, we'll be looking at point 3. We see: "Some of the forces of the 2-22 lpbr shall block the enemy forces on the village of Dabovci." Is this referring to the 2nd Battalion of the 22nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Judging by the order it was the 2nd Battalion of the 22nd Brigade. However, I repeat, I never received orders from any of the commanders who were not my immediate superiors. I never received any such orders, nor did I ever carry out any such orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, I think you misspoke. It's not Dabovici but Dabovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You're quite correct, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, sir, in terms of an operation, if I'm understanding your answer correctly, you would have received orders from Janko Trivic that you would then issue to your battalion if -- in operating as part of this operation, or in conducting your unit's portion of this operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: No, not correct. I did not receive any orders for this operation from Commander Trivic. There was no action at all. We were in our deployment sector near Vasiljevici. There was a company there over a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Are you saying, then, that the order on our screen is mistaken with respect to the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know whether there's a mistake here or not. I suppose that the commander of the 1st Kotor Varos Brigade issued an order to his own brigade and according to the methodology he was also duty-bound to provide information to the neighbouring units. In this particular case, I was one of his neighbours. Maybe this was just to copy us and to provide us with the information for reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I want to shift gears and talk about your involvement in the meetings of the Kotor Varos War Presidency relating to Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have P2884 on our screens, please. We'll be looking for page 4 in the English, page 3 in the B/C/S. This is an extract from the minutes of an extraordinary session of the Kotor Varos War Presidency held on 1 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move on, what we looked at earlier, that document which was shown to you and which described some operations, was -- from the geography you could see there, was that in the Vecici area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand your question. What do you mean? Which part are you referring to when you say whether it was in the Vecici area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps go back to the document --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could -- P440. And I believe page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we have it now before us. It starts in paragraph 1 with a reference to the citizens of the village of Vecici, et cetera. Then specifically I think your attention was drawn to paragraph 3: "Some of the forces of the 2-22 Light Infantry Brigade shall block the enemy forces on the villages of Dabovci ..." I'm talking about those areas. Is that the Vecici area or is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I understand, Your Honour. The axis involving Dabovci and Vasiljevici villages may be put in direct connection with the village of Vecici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you were asked about August 1992 to November 1992, and you said in answer -- in answering a question by

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: "During that period, there was no combat until the moment people left Vecici." Do I have to understand that this all happened when the people left Vecici or ... I'm trying to understand where this is -- what happened here, whether this preceded the people leaving Vecici or whether it was simultaneous or whether it happened after. Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I wanted to say and this is the truth, that this order -- I mean, the 2nd Battalion did not carry out this order, and I don't think that the 2nd -- or the 1st Light Kotor Varos Brigade ever carried out all the tasks that are mentioned in here. And I repeat, the date of the order precedes the departure of soldiers and civilians from Vecici village. And I repeat, the 2nd Infantry Company of the 2nd Battalion had been deployed in the Vasiljevici sector, which is a Serbian village bordering on the village of Vecici. It was there from before, and it did not carry out any special combat activities pursuant to this order at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you said there was no combat, not specifically you're referring to any specific unit; whereas if I read this document, it is seems that at least some combat orders were given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But this document didn't mean that a combat order was issued to the battalion. It could not have been. This order was issued by the commander of a different unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you said there was no combat in Vecici. And I said -- again, you didn't say this unit did not -- was not involved in combat or that unit was not involved in combat. You just said there was no combat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around those days, there was no combat in Vecici at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm still puzzled by the fact that you say what we see in paragraph 3 is the Vecici area. It very much looks to -- that it's combat orders to whatever unit, and I do not then fully understand why you say that there was no combat in the Vecici area where this document apparently orders -- give orders for attack. I'm just trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not the only case or a rare case that some orders for combat were not carried out. The period from the moment an order is issued to the eventual operation may give rise to various situations. That's exactly what happened here because there were intense negotiations going on about the departure of the population from Vecici village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your explanation is it may have been ordered but it did not happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a possible option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you say there's no combat, and if you say, I think it didn't happen, then it looks as if you're not certain whether these combat orders were followed, yes or no. And you again emphasised this by saying, This is what possibly was the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure, I'm sure, that the 2nd Battalion did not carry out any combat operations pursuant to this order. When I said that it was possible, I meant the orders that were issued to the units of the 1st Light Kotor Varos Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that you had contact with Colonel Novakovic every day from November 1st through at least November 5th as this operation was being carried out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: We were in contact around those days and even earlier as commanding officers of the neighbouring units.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, if we could go now to P2884, page 4 in the English, page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, the document that will come up is an extract from the meetings of an extraordinary session of the War Presidency, Kotor Varos, held on 1 November 1992. Now, at the top of the document, you're noted as being present at this meeting. We also see Captain Balaban was at this meeting on 1 November. He was a security and intelligence officer in the 1st Krajina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I was at that meeting, as well as some other meetings of the War Presidency when the brigade commander informed me, told me, that I should go. Captain Balaban also attended meetings that I attended. I know that he was a member of the security organs of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, as such, Captain Balaban would have reported back to the 1st Krajina Corps command about the events in Kotor Varos; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Probably. Although I was not aware of what Captain Balaban's authorities and competences were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In this document we see that Djekanovic, the War Presidency president, discusses current issues --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Djekanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Djekanovic discusses the current issues involving Vecici including those that have arisen from the corps command's prohibition against allowing civilians out of Vecici before all had laid down their arms. We see in this document that you state that you wanted an order issued to you via the chain of command with instructions on what to do. Now there had been a recent change in your command structure in the weeks prior to this meeting; correct? Perhaps I could be --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Not absolutely correct. There wasn't a change in the command structure -- structure a few weeks before. It was only one week before that that happened. A change in the command structure happened on the 23rd or the 24th of October. From the 24th of October to the 1st November, it is only six or seven days.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. And that would be that Janko Trivic, who we've discussed before, assumed command of Colonel Peulic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, Janko Trivic wore two hats. He took over the command of the 22nd Infantry Brigade from Peulic. At the same time he was the commander of Vlasic OG.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that the previous brigade commander, Peulic, had been replaced in part because of his failure to resolve Vecici?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure that that was the main reason. I think that a lot of things happened that led to Trivic and Peulic changing places.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you would agree that the failure to resolve Vecici was one of those factors?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: As far as I knew, I wasn't aware that the corps commander was dissatisfied by Peulic's command but I allow for that possibility to have been possible -- to have been present as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note we've just slightly passed the time for the morning break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break. Witness, you may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could now turn to page 3 in the English. If we could turn to page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, we'll see November -- 2 November 1992, continuation of an extraordinary War Presidency session. And we see Colonel Bogojevic referenced here. Now he was the assistant commander of the 1st Krajina Corps for security and intelligence; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I think Colonel Bogojevic was assistant commander of the 1st Krajina Corps for security. I'm not sure, though, whether he was in charge of intelligence as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And here, we see him stating: "He had received explicit orders from General Mladic that no one was allowed -- was to be allowed to leave Vecici until the unconditional surrender of weapons was completed." In the second-to-the last paragraph, we see Major Trivic telling the War Presidency: "President, that he should try to convince Karadzic that the only right way to solve Vecici was to push for unconditional surrender." Now, you supported that position; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I was in favour of the option agreed upon at one of the previous sessions of the War Presidency. It was to the effect that they should be offered to surrender their weapons, to have those captured delivered, as well as the corpses delivered to our side, and then everyone from Vecici was to be allowed to leave freely wherever they wanted to, in case they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So is that -- is your answer, yes, that you wanted to push for an unconditional surrender of Vecici?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: It was the decision of the military command and I was duty-bound to honour the decisions of my superior command. That is why in this situation I had previously asked for the following. Given the fact that there were different interpretations of how that situation was supposed to be dealt with, I asked that I receive direct instructions from my superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you supported what your military commanders told you to do; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: No. It wasn't up to me to support. It was up to me to implement the orders of my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were you there when the Muslim representatives from Vecici were brought in as described was going to happen in this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I think I was. I don't recall it in detail because it was a long time ago, but I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We'll now turn to P3743, which is an extract of the meeting of the War Presidency of Kotor Varos held on 3 November 1992. And I see the B/C/S document has come up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'll confirm that you were at this War Presidency session as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Under item 2 in the second paragraph, it states that you briefed the War Presidency of a report that the soldiers from Vecici had abandoned the village as had the civilian population. My question is: Did you provide this briefing as opposed to the others who were present because you were most heavily involved in the operations against Vecici?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Not because of that. As you can see, this is an extract from the minutes and it does not reflect the entire course of the War Presidency's session. It only provides highlights. It is correct that I did acquaint the War Presidency with the situation. According to the information arriving from the 2nd Company and other units, the battalion command was informed that the village was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now we'll turn to P852. This is an excerpt from the minutes of the 116th Kotor Varos War Presidency meeting on the 4th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And you would agree that you were present for this session as well; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And if we look at item 2, it states that you reported to the War Presidency regarding several things, including the surrender of 150 soldiers and civilians from Vecici. Was this something the War Presidency was unaware of at the time of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't think it was something that the War Presidency was unfamiliar with. I did not submit a report to the War Presidency. I was not under any obligation to do so. As the unit commander I was supposed to report to my superior command. I simply informed the War Presidency about the knowledge I gathered in between the two sessions of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, you've answered that as unit commander you were supposed to report to your superior command. You -- did you, in fact, report to your superior Janko Trivic that the 150 men had been captured?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes. When I received that information, I personally informed Trivic, the brigade commander, about the information I had received from the commander of the 1st Light infantry Kotor Varos Brigade, Colonel Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you also report to your superior that there were women in this group of individuals who surrendered?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: At the meeting of the battalion command, I forwarded the information I had received from Colonel Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did that include information that there were women in the group who had surrendered?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, it also included that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And there were children in the group that had surrendered; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I can't say anything with any certainty that there were children as well, but there were people who were younger in terms of age. That is definitely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, younger is a very relative concept. What was your information about age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information I received from Colonel Novakovic stated that there were 150 persons involved, including fighters, as well as civilians, such as women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it's now the second time -- first, when Ms. Bibles asked you whether you reported that there were women in this group, you said: I reported what I knew. That's not an answer to the question. It was only after the second question that you said: Indeed, I reported that there were women in the group. So that should have been your answer to the first question already. Now here we have the same. You say: Younger in age. I do understand that you had received information that there were children in the group. Why not answer that question directly and only in the second round? Could you please keep that in mind. Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you also report that the men had given up their weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently the witness said something which was not translated. Could you repeat what you said, Witness? Or was it the beginning of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked why I didn't say the first time around that there were women and children. What I said was that I informed my command about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Stop. We heard exactly what you said, and I invited you to directly answer questions and to keep that in mind. Listen carefully to the next question of Ms. Bibles and answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you also report that the men in this group --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did you also report that the men in this group had given up their weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, going back to the document in front of us, if we look at the next paragraph, we see that Pejic states that the organisation of a departure convoy should take place as soon as possible, and then: "Pejic, Zupljanin, Balaban, and Novakovic shall decide on the fate of the soldiers who were taken prisoner." Now to be very clear, this refers to the 150 men being held now at Grabovica; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: One would conclude so from the way this sentence was constructed although that could not have been the case in any respect. I could not have been someone who could decide on anything in that regard for at least two reasons. One reason was that it did not take place in the deployment area of the 2nd Battalion. And the second reason was that I could decide on such things only on -- if on strict orders from my superior command. Not from somebody else --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness mentioned a specific name at the very end of his answer which we did not catch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: At the end of your answer, you gave a name that we did not catch in the record. Could you repeat that name.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Pejic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, you would agree that the men, the people being held at Grabovica, were the responsibility of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: The VRS was responsible for them, among others, because they were in the deployment area of the 1st Light Infantry Brigade of Kotor Varos, which was part of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now Captain Balaban, the 1st Krajina Corps security officer, appears to have remained on scene starting with the negotiations that we first discussed in your cross-examination through the capture of these men from Vecici and was still present with you at this meeting which occurred on the 4th of November, 1992, discussing the captured men. Did he stay near you during these days?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Not only in the course of those few days but even before that he used to come to the deployment area frequently. Thus, I think he could have been present.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I want to go back to something that you volunteered up at line 10 through 12 on temporary page 30. You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you put to the witness that according to this document that Mr. Balaban was present, isn't it? Where do I see that in the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: In the reference to -- and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, was Captain Balaban present on that date? This document refers to the fact that Pejic, Zupljanin, Balaban, and Novakovic shall decide on the fate of the prisoners. Does that mean that Balaban was present?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I expected to answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: In and of itself it doesn't need necessarily be so, but I know that Balaban did attend some Presidency sessions and participated in the discussions on that topic in the course of those days.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness needs to move back and away from the microphone. The plosives are too much and we cannot make out the sounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, if could you sit back a slight distance more from the microphone that would enable the people translating to understand you a little bit better. We might make some adjustments here. Now, we didn't catch the end of your answer. You were talking about: "... but I know that Balaban did attend some Presidency sessions and participated in the" -- and then we were not able to understand your answer. Could you finish your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I think in the course of those few days, he attended most of the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you know where he was working from during those few days when he wasn't at the meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, in part of your answer, on page 30, I believe, lines 10 through 12, you indicated that the decision which is referenced in this document, that you would not be able to make that decision, that it would be based -- your decision would have to be based on something from superior command. Does that accurately state who would have made the decision about the fate of these soldiers? It would have been from superior command?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: It is beyond dispute that I could not make any decision in that regard. When I answered your question, I said that I could only receive an order from my superior command and on such orders I would be duty-bound to act. As far as responsibility goes, Colonel Novakovic, according to my knowledge and according to his statement, he said he was up there. That's what he told me. In that regard, he could have been the person responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We'll move now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, could we in questions and answers - I'm also addressing you, Witness - make a clear distinction between how things should have been and how they were. The fact that you can't do anything without instructions doesn't mean that you never do something without instructions and orders. Could we clearly make a distinction between the two. And, apart from that, could you tell us when you refer to the statement of Novakovic, which statement were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to his statement about those events surrounding the surrender of the 150 people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Statement given to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard him say that. I heard it from Colonel Novakovic. He presented it as information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you say "his statement," you are referring to what he told you? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And not to any statement taken for purposes of proceedings or any testimony given during proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I also have a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you said that the fate of those soldiers could have been decided only from -- by orders from above. Is it your position that whatever happened to anybody who was captured happened on orders from above? Is that -- was that a rule within the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One couldn't say that it necessarily had to be that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Therefore, it could happen that people lower down could decide the fate of captured soldiers without having received orders from above.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not what I meant. What I meant was that, in theory, there were such situations when an order from a superior command needed not be implemented if it ran counter to the laws and international conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you tell me one such incident where such order was not carried out because it ran counter to the laws of international conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any such experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now if we could move to 65 ter 31887.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: As it comes up on the screen, you will see that it is an extract from the minutes of the War Presidency of Kotor Varos of 5 November 1992. Would you agree that this would have been the day after the men at Grabovica had been killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: A day before or a day after.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Do you believe -- well, based on the information that you had at the time, isn't it true that the men were killed on the 4th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: This could have been either on the 3rd or on the 4th; I'm not entirely sure. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, Madam Registrar informs me that 65 ter 31887 may be a mistake. Apparently not being the document you're seeking to have on the screen. Perhaps you move on and try to find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have 31887 on our screens, please. And take a look at what the document -- it's coming up on our e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar informs me that she has no results on searching for 31887. Yes, but that has changed over the last few seconds, apparently, and now it is in the system. So let's have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: All right. Sir, we see this is the 5 November 1992 meeting of the War Presidency. We see that you're present; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And there's no mention of the 150 men who had been discussed in -- at least in the day before; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: The minutes do not reveal any number.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, the -- the last item states that a commission for war booty is to be set up. I can tell you that this Chamber has heard evidence that the valuables of the people who surrendered at Grabovica were left on the ground where they surrendered. Do you know, having been present at this meeting, whether this commission was being set up in response to those items?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know why the commission was set up. I know that it was set up. It was sent to the field, as far as I know, and they collected those items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, I think the English translation doesn't cover everything which is to be seen on the -- on the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: You're quite right, Your Honour. I will -- we will submit this for translation. I will not tender it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but apparently the witness has answered the question on the basis of what he could read. And, therefore, for the Chamber to understand the evidence of the witness because he said no number was mentioned. And I was about to ask him why there was no reference to even persons being killed, apart from numbers, and I have difficulties in putting that question to the witness, not knowing what the document tells us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Witness, was I -- were the 150 men discussed in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I can't remember whether they were or not. But I know something else. Previously Colonel Novakovic told me that he had informed the president of the War Presidency and some of its members about that. I can't remember the entire discussion that took place at that session, not fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will submit this for translation. I agree that it's not satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let's ... yes, we'll wait for that. Now, you said Colonel Novakovic had told you that he had informed the president of the War Presidency and some of its members about that. What are you referring to exactly with "that"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean the event which had taken place in Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is that a large number of men were killed? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, that people either surrender or were captured, because Colonel Novakovic first mentioned fighting and then he said that a certain number of people had surrendered. So I would say that it refers to both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you are talking about fighting and about surrendering. I'm talking about being killed. Could you please answer that question, whether that was what Novakovic had told the president of the War Presidency? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judging from what he told me, he referred to that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, the same question: Why not answer that -- why not give that answer right away instead of going around it for two or three times. Now, was that discussed during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now, I wouldn't say that I went around it. I can't remember of any of the details mentioned at the session itself, but I believe that it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if I say you are going around that question, that's a comment, not a question, and not the beginning of a debate. Could you tell us, could you answer my next question, then, whether this was at all mentioned during this meeting of the War Presidency on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The killing. I mean the killing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we'll then later find -- but perhaps the witness could tell us already. He can read it. Do you read in the version in your language any reference to such killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not here. I'd like to say this is just one excerpt from the minutes which does not reflect the entire discussion. It is just an excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. But you've answered my question, that it is not found in the minutes as -- the extract from the minutes as we have it before us. Mr. Lukic, you're in a better position to see what is there and is not there. I'm not asking you to -- at this moment to give any evidence, but perhaps during the break or you could assist or any native speaker could assist Ms. Bibles to know what we are looking at because the Chamber doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would suggest perhaps we just have the witness read item 2 in the original language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's really against what we are supposed to do, because our interpreters are not translators. But, now, under these exceptional circumstances, I'll ask the witness to slowly read. But, again, Ms. Bibles, this is not how we should operate. And, of course, I will be blamed by the interpreters for not following the rules of this Tribunal in this respect. But perhaps we could ask the witness to slowly read it and we do not expect the interpreters to do anything else than to interpret, and it's not a verified translation which we'll receive. Witness, could you slowly read, and upon the instructions of Ms. Bibles, remaining portions of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If could you just read item 2 to us, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why don't we start with item 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 2 ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, any reason why we should not start with item 1?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Most likely it is the approval of the minutes of the 116th -- if -- or everyone agrees that that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It would be better if it's read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness first read item 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Item 2 [as interpreted]: Excerpt from the minutes of the 116th meeting of the War Presidency." It was adopted without any objections. "Item 2: Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic reported to the War Presidency about the situation in the field as it was in the course of the day yesterday. He pointed out that combat operations were taking place in Duboka last evening and that today the clearing up of the area needs to be carried out. Savo Tepic informed about a convoy that was organised and passed through safely. Zarko Mikic emphasised that the clearing up of the terrain in Grabovica should be carried out."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you also then read item 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Item 3: As part of this item, there was a debate about military conscripts who were not assigned to any units. A conclusion was made that the commission should be set up which would make a list of the war booty. The session ended at 8.15."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Bibles, I think that we need an official translation of this document. And I think it's important to -- I don't know whether you intended to tender it, but there is an emphasis apparently on the necessity of "asanacija" which may be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask to MFI this document pending the official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Full translation. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31887 receives MFI P7090, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now if we could have P3705 on our screens, please. This is an extract of the minutes of the 6 November 1992 Kotor Varos War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the P number? It's not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. P3705.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: We see that you're present for this meeting. And I'd like to direct your attention to the end of item 2: "Djekanovic advises that he was in Grabovica the day before, monitoring the clearing of the terrain and the cleaning of the school." Sir, based on the information you have, is it your understanding that at least some of the men who surrendered were killed inside the school at Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, and I based that on the information that I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were more details about the massacre or about its clean-up discussed in more detail in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't think that there was a detailed conversation about that at the session. As you can see from the documents, and I heard that from Colonel Novakovic, the War Presidency and its members were abreast of all the developments.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, did you report to Janko Trivic that the 150 men had been killed in Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I reported to Colonel Trivic. I don't know whether I mentioned any figures, but I remember literally that based on the information that I had, the idiots up there caused a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Now, you knew that these killings were a crime; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I called the event a massacre at the time because I did know that a crime had been committed, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Did Trivic tell you to preserve the scene or scenes for an investigation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Trivic only asked me whether members of my unit had participated in that. I said no. And then he said that he would have a word with Colonel Novakovic about that. In other words, I was not instructed to do anything that would preserve the scene intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So to the best of your knowledge, is it true that there was never any investigation on the part of the VRS into the killings of the 150 men at Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I know that I informed Colonel Trivic about that, and I really don't know what he did next.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'd now like to go to 65 ter 31911. As this comes up -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you informed Colonel Trivic about the massacre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had learned that from whom exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Colonel Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you yourself do anything in order to -- to promote that the matter would be investigated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did what I was supposed to do. I informed my superior commander along the command line, and then Colonel Trivic should have informed the corps command. I don't know whether he did or not. I know that at the session of the War Presidency, we all condemned the whole thing, and we all demanded that an investigation should be carried out with this regard and that certain commissions should be set up. I don't know whether those commissions were ever set up or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you said you demanded that an investigation would be carried out and you told that the War Presidency. First of all, were you certain that your own subordinates had nothing to do with that crime -- those crimes committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was certain because they were not there. Physically they were not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said you demanded that an investigation would be carried out. What we see in the minutes of the War Presidency is, first, that there's an insistence on cleaning everything and there's a report the day after that the school was cleaned. Did you not say anything like: This is not what an investigation should be, to clean and wipe out all the possible traces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know who was going to do it or when. I didn't know who was going to do sanitation and hygiene activities. It was not my part of my duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We do not find anything in the minutes that there was any urging that an investigation would take place. As a matter of fact, what we see is rather the contrary. Could you tell us whether there's any documentary support for you urging that an investigation should take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe you misunderstood me. I did not do that personally. I told you that we discussed at the War Presidency session. It was not me personally who asked for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: "We all demanded that an investigation should be carried out." "We all," in my view, would include you, yourself, if you were present. But could you then tell us where we can find anything which would support your testimony that all demanded that an investigation would be carried out? Because the documents, as we see it now, points rather to the contrary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only document that might perhaps corroborate my words would be the entire minutes, not just an excerpt from the minutes. And I say maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you'd say -- is there anything more, Ms. Bibles, than just the extract of the minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not that you're aware. I'm also -- okay. Apparently we do not know whether it would give support but it's not available. Do you have any knowledge about where that could be found, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the then-War Presidency that was in charge of the minutes. I don't know what happened to all those documents, where they all ended up. In any case, as far as I know, the documents at one point were stored in the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bibles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 31911 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, this is a 5 November 1992 article that features an interview with you. Looking at page 1 in the B/C/S, I believe it's page 2 in the English, you've been quoted as saying it was a victory for the intelligence of the Army of Republika Srpska. And about six lines down in the English, and I apologise I'm not sure where it is in the original language, you speak about leading what you describe as Muslim fanatics to thin ice. In the next sentence you say: "That is how they met the fate they deserved." This is referring to the men from Vecici; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: The extremists from Vecici, not the entire population.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Were you quoted accurately here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you ask that, you should direct the attention of the witness to the respective article. There are three articles on that page. Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes. The article starting ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, I believe it's the article that's encaptured in the box on the page in front of you. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we enlarge that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely can't see this. The letters are too small.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll expand it. Can you read it now or does it need to be expanded further?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: A bit further, please. And now I can't see the entire text. Can you zoom out just a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And it's in the left column in the space below the bolded --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: It's good now. I can see it now. Scroll down a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Further. I think you can put your question now because it's the second -- the paragraph on the left side, not in bold.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, now that you've had an opportunity to read the places on which you were quoted, can you tell us whether you were quoted accurately?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: In principle, this would have been more or less what I said. And when we're talking here about people, those would be extremists. Further on, you will see what my position was towards the elderly, women, and children. Our military target were the extremists, not the elderly, the women, or the children.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Well, sir, with respect to the 150 men who you've already testified their killing was a crime, can you tell us if you have information as to where their bodies have gone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: There was some very generalised information about all that, but there was a veil of secrecy around all that. Not a lot was said. I heard from somebody - I can't remember from whom - that those bodies were buried somewhere in the direction of Plitska.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Moloto has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, you say according to this document and I hope -- I'll read what I see here and then you can tell me whether it's correct quotation from you. You say: "That is how they met the fate they deserved." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What it reads in my version is that: "And so the extremists received the punishment they deserved."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the punishment that was meted out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
