utterances.text: [Interpretation] The extremists were punished in such a way, from our point of view, was that they be liquidated or taken prisoner. Only in my battalion some 60 soldiers were killed and 100 were wounded by those extremists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I stop you there -- can I just stop you there. You're saying it was supposed to be that they be liquidated or be taken prisoner. I'm not asking you what the options were. I asked what became of them. Were they liquidated or were they taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my knowledge, some were eliminated and others taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "eliminate"? Do you mean liquidate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, these people had been taken prisoner. Isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some extremists were killed in the fighting conducted against the units of the 1st Light Infantry Kotor Varos Brigade and the 1st Knezevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about those -- I'm talking about these, these that you would not allow to leave Kotor Varos unarmed -- armed. You had to disarm them and then having been disarmed, you said they got liquidated, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You misunderstood. Some of those extremists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't -- just a second, please. I'm reading this document in which you are being quoted. You are quoted as having said: "Our expectations have come true. Since we did not let the Muslim fanatics leave the Kotor Varos armed although they had claimed that they would only need them in Travnik due to the more and more frequent conflicts between Croatian and Muslim armies," and then it goes on. And now, after that, that's when you then say that is how they met the fate they deserved. So you didn't allow them to leave armed and then you send them to their fate which was, as you explained, liquidation. Is that correct? Do I understand that article correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you did not understand it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just tell me how I must understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be understood in this way. Not 150 people left Vecici but many more. They were in several groups --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This document doesn't mention any number. We're talking about here about Muslim fighters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a news report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Precisely. And it's not talking about any numbers. It's talking about Muslim fanatics which you have said to Madam Bibles those were fanatics and they were not the people -- the civilians. Therefore they had to meet this fate that they deserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist only. There is a number, but upper in this text it is mentioned 500 extremist fighters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and 60 killed in combat. So there are numbers and maybe you should see the whole text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I don't see that. And may I be shown that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps in the previous page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the upper part of B/C/S as well. Maybe it should be shown to the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then in B/C/S it should be scrolled up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can see the number of 500. That notwithstanding, my question still stands. The number of the Muslim fanatics may or may not be less than the 500, but I'm just asking about the Muslim fanatics who met this fate of liquidation, whatever their number. Can you explain to us how we must understand that part of the article where it talks about disarming them and then sending them to their fate. Just can you explain --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the military target were the extremists. Those extremists needed to be prevailed over and eliminated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I stop you. We don't have much time. I understand that they were military targets. What I'm saying is, you have now disarmed them and you have told us a few minutes ago that they either had to be liquidated or be taken prisoner, so they are now no longer in combat. They are now prisoners. But then you decided they must be liquidated and they were liquidated. My question is: How else do we have to understand this part and your own evidence on this point? You've told us they were liquidated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the extremists needed to be either liquidated or taken prisoner. They were a legitimate military target and that's where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your have told us that. You've told us that and we have gone past that. You've told us that in fact between liquidation and taken prisoner, they were actually liquidated. You have told us that. So whatever you say, please don't repeat what you've already told us. Now, I see you're keeping quiet. I'm going to ask you my next question. My next question is: Was it within the laws -- can I ask my question. Was it within the international conventions that you referred to earlier to liquidate them because they were fanatics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must explain briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Answer my question first, answer my question before you explain. Then you can explain after answering my question. Was it within international conventions to liquidate them because they were fanatics? Yes or no. And then you can explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you said I could explain. It is unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I first inform you that this is a testing which takes place every first Monday of the month at 12.00. So don't be worried about the sirens. Then now please explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So -- so under the punishment they preserved [as interpreted] is to be liquidated during combat. It pertained to the extremists. It also pertained to being taken prisoner. I did not want to place anything else under the concept of punishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are not explaining the point. You tried to explain why you say no, it is not within the legal -- international conventions to do so. My next question: Who liquidated them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the information I received from Colonel Novakovic, when he said that there was a terrible incident there which primarily included Serbian civilian population, he said that his security and his soldiers were unable to prevent that incident from taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In your mind, now that you said this is not according to international conventions, would you regard this kind of killing of these people a crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if anyone of those people who killed them was arrested and went through the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic -- Mr. Lukic, could you tell us how much time you'd need in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not more than 20 minutes, I hope I'll finish in 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break first and then you have an opportunity to re-examine the witness. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 25 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to come in, Mr. Lukic, I think the Chamber did not receive yet the information it wished to receive in relation to the expert witnesses, at least the information was too vague. Without going into details now, could you please consider whether you could, on shortest notice, give us whatever information you have or perhaps even not have yet but which you understand the Chamber would need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you'll now be re-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, once again, Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we have P440 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document has already been shown to you, dated the 30th October 1992. You said that there was no fighting before the civilians left. We see in item 1 that it states: "The citizens of the village of Vecici were given the opportunity to persuade the paramilitary formations to give up their weapons ..." And then further down it says: "The stand was taken to allow the departure and evacuation of the civilian population in exchange for the bodies of three dead soldiers and three captured soldiers of the VRS. The convoy with the population is to set out at 0700 hours on 1 November 1992." Do you know if a convoy was indeed organised that was supposed to carry civilians?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, a convoy was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, although there is combat operation referred to in the date -- in the document, it is stated that on 1 November the convoy was supposed to be organised. Do you know whether there was any fighting between the 30th of October and the 1st of November?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: My unit was not engaged in any combat operations but I'm not certain about the 1st Light Infantry Kotor Varos Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have P443 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will see an excerpt from the minutes of the War Presidency of Kotor Varos dated the 2nd November 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's P443.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the last paragraph we see that Captain Balaban brought representatives to negotiate from Vecici, and we see their names. And apparently they went back to Vecici. So on the 2nd of November when there were still negotiations under way, was there still combat or were there only negotiations happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, only the negotiations were under way at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at P ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not so well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll refrain at this moment from further dealing with the matter. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can see P2884 on our screens. [Interpretation] This document contains several excerpts from the minutes. While we are on this page, please look at the bottom of the page. Item 2 in the B/C/S. I apologise, item 3. In the English, it is at the very bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see that you were -- are taking the floor there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we need to move to the next page in English where the part I will be referring to is found.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see it at the very top of the English page and in the B/C/S, it is item 3, Captain S. Zupljanin. It is stated here that you pointed out the possibility of introducing a bus line to Siprage. And this discussion was taking place on the 2nd of November, 1992. Was it easy to organise a bus route at the time and is this something you were working on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: We were working on it, because there was constant communication with Siprage and I believe our communication with the civilian population there was excellent, with the representatives of Muslims from Siprage village. Of course, there were reasons for that. There was the will on the part of the civilians, residents of Siprage, to deal with the situation in Siprage incident free. It was also in the interests of the VRS because daily or weekly, at least once, parts of military units went through Siprage in order to reach their positions at Vlasic. Therefore, we established such links with them that throughout the period, the residents of Siprage move unhindered into the direction of Kotor Varos or elsewhere they wanted to go. By the same token, without any incidents our soldiers passed through the village en route to their positions. The situation was one of great mutual trust.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At this same time, do you know if there were ABiH formation members at Vasic who were from Siprage?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: We knew that from a reliable source. There was an attack on our positions between 12th and 14th of September, 1992. Among the killed Muslim soldiers in the sector of Rijecica were the corpses of several fighters from Siprage. However, for us it is not reason enough to cause any incident in Siprage. We simply continued developing good co-operation in order to preserve the peace and good atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to the situation in Vecici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the third page of this document in the B/C/S and the next page in the English version. Actually, two pages ahead in the English. It is an excerpt of the minutes from the 1st of November, 1992, from the meeting of the Kotor Varos War Presidency. Somewhere around the middle of the page in the B/C/S, we see: "Captain S. Zupljanin."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Slobodan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have "S. Zupljanin" here. It reads: "Captain S. Zupljanin remarked that previously he had wholly supported the earlier adopted solution to the question of Vecici ..." Tell us what were you against or what were you in favour of?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: We were in favour of the weapons being handed over and that everyone be allowed to leave Vecici if they so wished in whatever direction they wanted to go, under the condition I mentioned previously, which was that the bodies of three of our killed people were handed over as well as the three prisoners they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have P852, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will see an excerpt from the minutes of the Kotor Varos War Presidency dated the 4th of November. This was shown to you, where it says that the fate of the captured fighters will be decided by Pejic, Zupljanin, Balaban, and Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic. This is the 4th of November. In relation to it, let us look at P441, so do please bear in mind the task issued to the four people referenced therein on the 4th of November. Please bear with me. Before us is a report of the 1st Krajina Corps Command dated the 4th of November, 1992. It has already been reported in item 2, paragraph 2, that -- it's somewhere in the middle of the paragraph, that some 40 members of the Green Berets were killed and some 200 captured. "A brutal massacre of the captured members of the Green Berets started because of the wounding of four and the killing of one soldier of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade and the burning of wounded soldiers on Gola Planina (Jajce)." It was on the same day that you were issued the task by the War Presidency. Do you know that Pejic, Balaban, and Novakovic -- or whether the three had anything to do with the implementation of the task assigned to you as well on the 4th of November, 1992, to decide on the fate of these people?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Your interpretation is incorrect. We did not receive a task. Pejic, one of those present at War Presidency sessions, said that. It was his statement. It was not binding on either me or others. Pejic could not issue tasks to members of the army, in particular. I may exclude the police but certainly not the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is that I'm trying to show? On the 4th of November, when this discussion took place at the War Presidency, it is the same day when the report by the 1st KK Command was issued. By that time, the people had been killed, the day earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't know for sure, but I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's look at 65 ter 31887. I don't know if it has a P number. I've not made a note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is dated 5 November, an excerpt from the 117th Session of the War Presidency. You have already seen that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now P7090, MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have read out under item 2. Something hasn't been translated, therefore I'm going to read it to you: "Savo Tepic informed about a convoy that has been organised and passed through safely." How many groups of people withdrew from Vecici, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: According to the information that I had, some of the civilians withdrew from Vecici in a convoy from Vecici to Vrbanjci and then on to Kotor Varos and further on in the direction of Banja Luka. Those who did not opt for that kind of withdrawal and instead went in the direction of Jezica or, rather, the general sector of Grabovica and Skender Vakuf. According to the information that I subsequently received, they were withdrawing in three groups at least. Some of those engaged with members of the VRS, some of the units surrendered to the Knezevo Brigade, and some to the 1st Light Kotor Varos Brigade of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from those men who were killed in Grabovica, what about the transport of others? Was it uneventful or were there any problems as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, their transport was uneventful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have told us that you informed your commander, Trivic, about what Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic had told you; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Novakovic was the commander of the unit whose elements were deployed in Grabovica; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have also told us that the War Presidency was abreast of the killings in Grabovica; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As a battalion commander, the commander of a battalion that was not deployed in Grabovica, were you in a position to carry out an independent investigation at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: No, I couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Apart from briefing your own commander, were you duty-bound to brief or report to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: No, I was not duty-bound to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at the last document I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 65 ter number 31911. I don't have its P number, if it indeed has been given one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to the document but let's first look at the top of the page, and we can see that the newspaper was published on Thursday, 5 November 1992. And it says here: "Kotor Varos, 4 November," this is what the news item is about. Do you remember the date when you gave this interview?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: No, I can't remember the date with any reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you're talking about the liquidation of extremists, what liquidation did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I was talking about the liquidation of extremists who were liquidated in fighting with the Knezevo Brigade in the sector above Jezica in the direction of Knezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says here in the text that there were over 60 casualties on the side of Muslim fighters. As a matter of fact, I have no further questions about this particular document. Mr. Zupljanin, this was all I had prepared for you. Thank you for having answered my questions.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Bibles, you didn't tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Right. My appreciation to my colleague across the courtroom. I would now tender 31911.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number, Madam Registrar, would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 31911 receives Exhibit P7091, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Witness, before you give an opportunity to Ms. Bibles to put further questions to you, I have a question in relation to paragraph 19 of your statement wherein you emphasised that you were the first to prepare and send the superior command the report on the event at Koricanske Stijene where the 22nd Infantry Brigade played a positive role in the sense of providing help to the wounded. Could you -- you are not further elaborating on the event. Could you tell us exactly what you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the massacre of civilians from Prijedor at Koricanske Stijene, and that location is within the deployment sector of the 22nd Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you say you provided help to the wounded. There were not many wounded because most of them were killed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now - and I'm also looking at the Defence - you say that you have prepared and sent a report to the superior command. Is that anywhere in evidence, Mr. Lukic? Or is it -- because the Chamber, in order to better understand and analyse the evidence, would like to see how this report was -- what the text of that report is. Do you have a copy or -- was it a written report, to start with, as the first question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a copy of that report but I know for a fact that the written report was conveyed to the corps command through our communications means. Lieutenant-Colonel, or Colonel, Peulic and I discussed that subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now was your positive role set out there, or was the event in its entirety described? That is, with a lot of people apparently just executed, very few surviving. Now what did you report? Or do the parties have the report anywhere so that we could at least have a look at how it was reported? But perhaps the witness could tell us already and the parties meanwhile will search for whether there is a report available.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we learnt that the massacre had taken place, that the civilians over there had been killed - I'm talking about Koricanske Stijene - Peulic learnt about that, and he immediately sent some of the soldiers to the site of the incident. There were members of the scout detachment or the military police. They returned and told him that the civilian population had indeed been massacred over there. And then Peulic ordered the scouts and the military police to try and see what could be done in order to save the victims. I learned later on, not on that date, but indeed later on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But now what did the report say? Ms. Bibles. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could direct your attention to 65 ter 6644, which is a report of the 1KK from Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic regarding this event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We may have a look at it soon. What did you report? A massacre has happened. Many civilians were killed, were executed, but fortunately a few survived -- one second. But fortunately we were able to help the very few survivors. And is that the kind of report? Or was it: We learned about people being wounded and we went there to help them? Could you describe more or less what the gist of the report was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gist of the report was this: A crime or a massacre took place in the deployment sector of the brigade. A lot of people were killed. The brigade undertook measures in order to learn more and to possibly help the survivors. I believe that that was the gist of that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's ... one second, please. Yes, perhaps we get 65 ter 6640 on our -- was it 6640? Let me just a look. 6644 on our screen. Yes, I see the report indeed in very clear terms describes - we have it on our screen now - that refugees were taken out and genocide against the civilians was committed by killing them in various ways and throwing them into the river canyon. That is an unequivocal description of a massacre. Now I see that Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic did send this document. Is there any documentary support for your participation in the preparation and the sending of this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if there's any documentary support. When a report is handwritten, it is sent to the communications service of the unit, which then in its turn does what they need to do with the unit. The report is submitted to the commander, and it can be prepared by anybody in the unit who was given the task to prepare it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you said you prepared that report. Is that how I have to understand or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I provided the main determinants of that report, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and how did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody came to the command to talk to Peulic. He briefed us -- or him about the incident and then Peulic in his turn briefed all the others of us at the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's still not clear what then exactly your role was in that. The report is clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't play any particular role. When we learnt about that and when we realised what had happened, we immediately knew and were of the opinion that our superior command had to be told the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Mr. Lukic, I can imagine that this clearly supports -- at least that Peulic reported at some point in time, the time is a still a bit unclear because the date, whether it's August or not, it looks as if it's the 21st. Now it's my recollection that the -- could -- do the parties have a common opinion about on what date the Koricanske Stijene -- wasn't it the 28th of August?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I believe it was the 21st of August, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 21st of August. If it would be the 21st August, then it may be very likely that what is illegible which --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- looks a bit like it could be well be an 8 in the original, I would say. It also looks a bit like a 6. But the two do not contradict each other necessarily. Mr. Lukic, would this be a document you'd like to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we'd like to tender it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06644 receives Exhibit Number D888, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D888 is admitted into evidence. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour. I'd like to go back quickly to P852.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Sir, was it your recollection that most of the War Presidency meetings were early in the morning, around 8.00?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, in the early morning hours usually.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And we see on our screen the document Mr. Lukic referred to on the 4th of November, 1992, and this reflects 8.00 a.m. Is that consistent with your recollection of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And then if we could go to P441 which was also directed to your attention on re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And, sir, would you agree that the 1900 hours at the end of this report would suggest that this was the evening report submitted to the corps? I'm sorry, from the corps.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: I don't see that. 1900 hours?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: If you -- excuse me, sir, if you could look down at the bottom of the page in the little square.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Perhaps we could blow that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Inside the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Inside the stamp.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: Yes, it may be 1900 hours because the units used to submit their reports to the corps command by that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: So is it also reasonable to conclude from these documents that the killing of the 150 men occurred sometime after 8.10 in the morning and 1900 hours in the evening on the 4th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you after or do you say between?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now, Ms. Bibles, are you seeking a conclusion from this witness interpreting the documents? Is that what you are seeking from him? Ask him what he knows, and if you want to draw conclusions then, perhaps that's argument rather than --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I apologise. I was moving quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: Having seen these two documents and reflecting on your own knowledge at the time, do you believe that it's likely the men were killed during sometime between 8.10 in the morning and 1900 on the 4th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: You mean Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, referring to the men at Grabovica.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN ZUPLJANIN
utterances.text: It may have been during that interval, yes, because we didn't hear anything about that in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIBLES
utterances.text: And I have no further recross, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, I left it until the very last end of -- and perhaps ... yes, just to let you know -- do you have any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I -- then there's no problem perhaps in raising the matter. You asked the witness whether it was still negotiating rather than doing anything else, referring to P440. Now, of course, I've carefully listened to the answer of the witness but if I read in P444, under 2, the Kotor Varos 1st Light Infantry Brigade is carrying out an attack with some of its forces and then the whole thing is described there. Then, of course -- and we'll carefully consider the answer of the witness but apparently you did not put it to the witness and you should be aware that if you conduct your examination in such a way that you leave the Chamber to find out whether the document is the better or whether the evidence of the witness is the better evidence. I think P440, I think I have -- let me just check. I think it's P440. I just wanted to bring this to your attention, but since you had no further questions to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can maybe draw your attention, Your Honour - you can check in other documents of this kind - that it was present tense used for future actions in documents like this. And you can see in the document on the second page that the command post was envisaged to be established on 1st of 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's all fine but the language is pretty clear: Is carrying out --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- is present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- an attack and describes then what should be done according to the success of the action undertaken at that point in time in which Vecici is -- okay. I leave it to that, but just be aware that if you ask these questions, that, of course, the Chamber will not stop reading the documents. We leave it to that. Witness, I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties and put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher. I would prefer that the statement is returned to the party that has provided it, and that is the Defence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we first take a break. And then is the Defence ready to call its next witness after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we are ready, and we are calling Mr. Kolenda, Davor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we will take a break and resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kolenda, I presume. Mr. Kolenda, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you, and I'd like to invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Kolenda. Mr. Kolenda, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kolenda.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the assistance of the usher to hand the written statement to Mr. Kolenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kolenda, for the record, please, kindly tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Davor Kolenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And can we have 1D1705 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kolenda, did you provide a statement to members of General Mladic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In front of you on the screen and in hard copy is a document. Do you see a signature on it and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: I do, and it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to the last page now. It is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it yours?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have had occasion to go through the statement. Hence, I would like to ask you whether what is recorded in it is recorded accurately?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the statement accurately and truthfully reflect what you told us? Is it accurate and truthful?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: I provided a similar statement in July 1993, and I think the two are identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you answer the same way?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Given the fact that I was an eye-witness to these events, my answer is yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak up or approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please come a bit closer to the microphone or to speak slightly louder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, one of your questions were not answered. The question if the statement accurately and truthfully reflects what he has told.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kolenda, you heard the question. We are missing something in the transcript. The contents of this written statement, does it accurately reflect what you stated at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the witness referred to a statement in July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He said that he gave almost the same statement in 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But to who --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To some other organ, not to our [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do not know -- to whom did you give a statement in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the SIS service of the HVO. It is the security service of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. After this we would tender the statement of Mr. Kolenda into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01705 receives Exhibit Number D889, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D889 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I will just read the statement summary of Mr. Kolenda and I will not have questions for him at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In 1993, Mr. Kolenda held the positions of chief of general affairs and general secretary of HVO, Croat Defence Council of Travnik. Having been an official of the Croatian Defence Council in the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Kolenda will testify about the armed clashes between the Muslims and Croats in Central Bosnia and about the exodus of the Croat population from Central Bosnia on 7th of June, 1993. Mr. Kolenda tried to negotiate with UNPROFOR to help Croat population to safely leave the area of Travnik but UNPROFOR representatives refused to do so. Because of this, he started to negotiate with the Serb side the evacuation of the wounded and immobile civilians, the elderly, women, and children through the Serb-held territory. When the Muslims had cut off the road through Bukovica, a large number of military conscripts were heading towards Galica and Serb-held territory together with the civilians. He will speak about the movement of several thousand women, children, men, and soldiers across Mount Vlasic and Kupres, through the Serb territory, and about the humanitarian and medical aid provided by the Serbs during the passage. Davor Kolenda will explain that a military element of HVO was accommodated at Manjaca for several days during the above-described movement, until vehicles were provided for their further transport. He will testify that the accommodation was provided on humanitarian grounds and without any criminal motive, whereby he will refute the assertions of the expert, Witness Ewan Brown. On 12th of June, 1993, Croat soldiers were taken from Manjaca to Vares, Croat-held territory in B and H. That was the short summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have no further questions. Could you assist us, Mr. Lukic. Is it in general that the evidence refutes the assertions of Ewan Brown or is it specific portions which --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is specific portion of Mr. Brown's report regarding Manjaca, when he was describing that Manjaca was operating as a camp in 1993 as well and had in mind this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- placement of HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it is clear that it's about that portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, even when Mr. Lukic has no questions for you, it doesn't mean that your evidence is lacking importance in no way, but we have it in written form here. And you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Bos. Mr. Bos is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Bos, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kolenda. Sir, just prior to the outbreak of the military clash between the ABiH and the HVO in June 1993, you held the position in the Travnik government as minister of non-commercial sector information, general affairs, and refugees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And as the responsible person for refugee issues, I take it that you had access to and knowledge of data relating to the number of refugees that entered the municipality of Travnik in this period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you would have been aware that there was a mass flight from the Krajina in the period between the commencement of the conflict and mid-1993 and that more than 18.000 Bosnian Muslims from the Krajina area registered in Travnik municipality alone?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: According to my information, in early June 1993, there were 17.600 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Almost 18.000. And is it not true that these refugees from the Krajina were expelled on a daily basis from this area by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, it was already mentioned at the beginning, it's true that you also gave a statement to the HVO SIS, in effect it was on September -- the 2nd of September, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: I think it was in July, although I don't know when it was filed exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But we'll -- I'm going to show you the statement. But this statement is indeed almost identical verbatim to the content of your statement that you gave to the Mladic Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: I'd say 95 per cent identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And it's those 5 per cent that -- there's a couple of parts in that statement that were taken out and a couple of these parts that were taken out I would like to go through, over with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So I would ask the Registry to put on the screen 65 ter 31926.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And this will be your SIS statement. And maybe if I could direct you first to the last page, which is page 10 on the B/C/S version, and maybe you can confirm there if that's indeed the signature -- your signature on that page.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, I want next direct you to the B/C/S page number 7 and the English page number 8. And on the B/C/S page number 7 I'm referring you to the bottom sentence, and the English on page 8, which reads, and I'll read out the sentence: "I was asked to give an interview to the Banja Luka Television and to present the events in Travnik, which I did." Can you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: I must say that my sight does not allow me to read such small text, but perhaps with the usher's assistance, it could be enlarged. In any case, I did provide an interview for the Banja Luka TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's try and enlarge it and we should enlarge the bottom part of the statement because I'm talking about the one-but-last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You enlarged the English version but not the Croatian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: There, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is not sufficient. We could remove the English one for a while so that the witness is able to read an enlarged the B/C/S part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No need. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So is this large enough, Mr. Kolenda?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So as I said I'd like to refer you to the one-but-last sentence which says: "I was asked to give an interview to the Banja Luka Television and to present the events in Travnik, which I did." You read that sentence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we could again put the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, maybe if -- if we can leave it for one minute because I'm going to ask about the next sentence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But let me first ask you this: This request to give an interview to the Banja Luka Television, that was shortly made after you and all the civilians had been evacuated from Ovcarevo to the Serb-controlled area of Kalesija. Is that correct? And so this was on the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shouldn't we move to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the statement was given immediately after my arrival at Galica. I appeared at Galica with my escort following the protection unit's end of tasks. We followed them and a colleague of mine came as last there on the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this sentence just corresponds directly with paragraph 38 of your 92 ter statement. But the next sentence - and I'll read that one out to you - is a sentence that is not found back in your statement and this one reads: "The Serbs wanted to use that favour of their in media purposes and they wanted it." Now, the English translation is not very clear. Could you explain what you meant by that sentence in your SIS statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: I wanted to say what really happened in the field. That is to say, we needed assistance with evacuating civilians, the wounded, children, and a part of the armed force. The Serbs obviously used it for propaganda purposes in order to show the world that they respect international law and other elements of humanitarian law. They wanted to have it publicised for everyone to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And is it correct that after this interview that you gave to Banja Luka Television that you also gave a statement to Reuters press that day? And three days later that you were also giving statements at Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I would like to look at a press report that was issued after your arrival at Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31928 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, I hope we can enlarge it in such a way that can you read it, Mr. Kolenda. Now, this is an article - and we'll read that in the first part of the document - from a journalist called V. Dubocanin and it's dated the 15th of June, 1993. And it's entitled: "Davor Kolenda, Secretary-General of the Croatian Defence Council in Travnik, on genesis of Muslim Croat conflict in former Bosnia-Herzegovina: Evil of Bajram." Can you read that, that's in the first part of this document. Now, this article -- in this article you discuss in more detail the conflict between the Bosnian Muslims and the Croats in Travnik and you express your gratitude on how you came to agreement with the Serbs to save the Bosnian Croat civilians from Travnik from what you called in this interview the invasion of Islamic evil. Do you recall giving this interview to Mr. Dubocanin?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: When I reached Galica, which is on Mount Vlasic overlooking Travnik, I provided an interview to a TV crew brought there by the VRS. It lasted for about 45 minutes. In that TV interview, I explained the genesis of events from 1992, when the first incidents broke out involving the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, until the moment we were expelled from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, if I could direct you to the last part of this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And that will be page 2 of both the B/C/S and the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first have a -- Witness, you explained to us that you gave a TV interview. Was that an interview conducted by Mr. Dubocanin or was that another interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no idea who Mr. Dubocanin is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm directing your attention now to the last part of this interview in which are you quoted saying -- and I'll read out from the document. This is when you were being asked about your treatment in Manjaca camp, and you're saying: "We were actually nicely received and welcomed, and we owe the Serbs only gratitude. I have no criticisms whatsoever of the treatment in the receiving centre in Manjaca, where primarily members of the HVO were accommodated. They really treated us humanely." Is this what you told the media about your treatment of the HVO soldiers in Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: When I answered a moment ago, I said that it happened at Galica before Manjaca. As for this interview, 22 years later, I really do not recall it. However, in essence, it was so. I don't recall any interviews with Mr. Dubocanin, but there were many journalist crews at Manjaca and they all wanted a statement. Hence, I was unable to memorize the journalists or soldiers who wanted statements. In general, though, I can tell you now that as far as the treatment in the reception centre in Manjaca is concerned, it was correct. It was fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go back to your 1993 statement to the SIS in which you also talk about your treatment in the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So could the Prosecution please again have 65 ter 31926 on the screen. And this time I would like page 9 of this document of both the English and the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask again that the Croatian version be enlarged. I can follow it in English, but my mother tongue, of course, comes more naturally, and I say this in order to avoid any mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I hope we'll -- we'll [indiscernible] a bit and I'll read out the parts so that -- but hopefully is this big enough?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: Yes, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to the top of page 9 where it reads in: "In the meantime on 9 June 1992, we organised cleaning and we made latrines." Now this sentence corresponds with paragraph 43 of your present statement, but then the 1993 SIS statement continues and I'll read that out: "We were not eating anything at all from the time we set off to Kalesija until 10 June 1993. On 10 June 1993, we got the first meal which was a piece of bread and a bit of patty. On 11 June 1993 food from the regional office of Caritas in Banja Luka arrived, and almost all of us got diarrhea due to the milk from that shipment." If we continue reading this part of your SIS statement, we get to a sentence that is found back again in paragraph 44 of your present statement and reads: "The journalists came twice more and told us that the civilians were transferred to Croatia through Novsk." Your SIS statement then continues with a couple of paragraphs that were again not found back in your present statement, and I'll read them out again: "On 11 June 1993, the TV crew of the Serb army came and maltreated us the whole day, requesting us to shout together: 'Bosnia is Serbian as much as Moscow is Russian. We are the war prisoners of the Army of the Republic of Srpska. We are the HVO soldiers.' I officially protested against that maltreatment and the words we had to shout. I informed all the soldiers about it and they supported it." Now, Mr. Kolenda, when you say: "I informed all the soldiers about it and they supported it," which soldiers are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: All the soldiers, conditionally speaking, of approximately 882, as far as I can remember, and those men had arrived in the Manjaca collection centre. Some 500 had been members of the HV units and the HV police. The others were of military age, between the ages of 18 and 50, but they had not all been soldiers before. We were accommodated in two barns, some 450 in one and some 450 in the other. Those barns had their commanders. We were told that we should arrange our own life within the collection centre and that the Army of Republika Srpska would guard us. The barns had its two commanders, and then those commanders decided that I would communicate with the soldiers of the VRS and represent all the inmates. So I went to both of the barns, and together with their commanders, I informed them that I had lodged a protest as a result of the ill-treatment that lasted all day. I personally believe that it was not in accordance with any international rules and regulations. Well, I could have understood that they needed some sort of propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. And if you say that HVO soldiers supported your protest, does that mean that they all felt humiliated by the treatment of the VRS TV crew?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR KOLENDA
utterances.text: When somebody leaves you outside at a temperature of over 30 degrees centigrade and when you're asked to give a statement and say that Bosnia is Serbian as much as Moscow is Russian and when you go on repeating that so that you may be recorded from all the different angles, obviously it is humiliating. We were not real prisoners, as a matter of fact. We came to seek assistance there. We hadn't been captured in a proper military way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: At this stage, I would like to tender Mr. Kolenda's SIS witness statement under Rule 65 ter number 31926.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31926 receives Exhibit Number P7092 [Realtime transcript read in error "P7192"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I would also like to tender the press release under 65 ter 31928.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31928 receives Exhibit Number P7093, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7093 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Bos, I think we are at the time to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If I can make just one correction on the transcript because the transcript of the first -- the first exhibit reads "P7192" and it should read "P7092."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is hereby corrected. Yes, there's more wrong. I think that the words are spoken by Madam Registrar and not by myself so that has to be reviewed, that line, anyhow. Mr. Kolenda, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30, but before you leave this courtroom, I would instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever it may be about your testimony, that is testimony given today or testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that is clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 3rd of February, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
